To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the temporal structure of neocortical activity in the prefrontocortical region during slow oscillations is determined by two independent processes, one slow, related to the global activity of the network and the other fast, related to the intrinsic excitability of the cells.

the time course of ensemble activity during slow oscillations depends on both the time lag of the first cell firing and the session-averged firing rates of cells, which can be explained by two distinct processes: a slow process, modulating the firing time lag for each cell and a fast process related to global cell activity.

1) the time lag between UP onset and the first spike of each cell depends on the cell’s average firing rate; and 2) the time lag of the first spike is consistent across trials, but its variability increases when the firing rate of the cell is higher.

the UP state onset is characterized by a fast reinstatement of cell activity, which depends primarily on global activity levels, and by a slow process affecting the time course of cell firing.
the reinstatement of activity during UP states depends both on a slow, global, network-related process and a fast, cell-specific process.

the reinstatement of activity in a given neuron is the sum of two processes: one slow and cell specific (i.e., the temporal evolution of the firing rate), and one fast and cell independent (i.e., a global activity process).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the temporal structure of cortical activity during slow oscillations is the outcome of two processes with distinct time scales: the slow process is the one that modulates the temporal structure of the activity, while the fast process is responsible for its reinstatement.
the time structure of cortical cell activity during UP states can be described as the result of two distinct processes, each of them acting on a different time scale.

the temporal structure of neocortical activity is the result of two different processes: (a) a slow, network-dependent process that modulates the temporal course of each cell firing, and (b) a fast, global process that determines when cells fire.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the temporal structure of neocortical activity at the onset of UP states can be explained by two distinct mechanisms: one slow, possibly related to network dynamics, and one fast, related to the global activity of the network.
, at the population level, the temporal structure of UP states is primarily determined by the session-averaging firing rates of cells, which in turn can be explained by the Poisson model.
, during SWS, cells are not simply driven by the network, but also actively participate in the reinstatement of neocortical activity.
